title: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear Challenge to Trump's Border Asylum Ban
excerpt: The justices will decide whether President Trump's January 2025 proclamation lawfully shut off asylum at the southern border — a policy two lower courts rejected but that remains in force, with a ruling expected by summer 2027.
body:
• The Supreme Court agreed on November 13 to hear Mullin v. RAICES, the challenge to President Trump's proclamation barring asylum claims by people who cross the southern border outside ports of entry.
  • The ban, in force since January 20, 2025, stays in place while the case proceeds — nothing changes for asylum seekers today. Arguments are expected in spring 2027, with a decision by the end of June or early July 2027.
  • Two lower federal courts rejected the administration's argument; the D.C. Circuit ruled the proclamation unlawful to the extent it blocks migrants already inside the United States from applying for asylum.
  • Border Patrol recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline from more than 1.8 million a year under President Biden, according to CBP data cited by NPR.

For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Now the Supreme Court will decide the central legal question behind those moves: whether a president can, on his own authority, suspend access to asylum protections that Congress wrote into federal law. NPR's report traces how the case reached the court and what rides on it.

Who is affected, exactly

The case concerns people who cross the southern border outside authorised ports of entry and seek asylum in the United States. Presidential Proclamation 10888, issued on January 20, 2025 — within hours of President Trump retaking office — declared a border emergency and suspended that access. The D.C. Circuit's ruling against the administration covered migrants already inside the United States who are blocked from applying and face removal through procedures the challengers say Congress never wrote. The Supreme Court granted review on November 13, limited to two questions: whether the proclamation and its implementing guidance are lawful, and whether a federal statute, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), bars the class-wide relief the lower court issued, according to coverage of the court's order.

What changed, and the mechanism behind it

Under the asylum system Congress created, a person who reaches U.S. soil can apply for protection from persecution, and an immigration judge weighs the claim. The proclamation displaced that process at the border. NPR reports the administration has also urged ICE attorneys to terminate pending asylum claims by arguing applications are incomplete or unsubstantiated, or that the person could apply in a third country instead — a strategy the Department of Homeland Security has used to cancel thousands of pending cases. National asylum denial rates reached 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024, according to TRAC, a Syracuse University research project that tracks immigration court data.

The immigration courts themselves have been remade. The administration has purged more than a hundred experienced immigration judges; nearly 40% of judges were fired or resigned during Trump's first year back in office, and more than half of the bench is now made up of Trump appointees, NPR reports. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago who was fired by email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench, told NPR: "Everything is different now." According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued during the second Trump administration, compared with 30 immigration-court memorandums across Biden's four-year term.

"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger. The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger."

— Lee Gelernt, Deputy Director, ACLU Immigrants' Rights Project

The administration's case

In legal filings, the administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and against abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow at the Heritage Foundation's Border Security and Immigration Center, told NPR that "the difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," and that reversing the ban "would be disastrous." He contends most people arriving at the southern border do not qualify for asylum. The administration's solicitor general petitioned the Supreme Court in August to overturn the D.C. Circuit ruling.

What happens next

The ban remains in force while the case is briefed and argued — the grant of review is not a ruling on the merits, and no hearing date has been set. Arguments are expected in spring 2027, with a decision anticipated by the end of June or early July 2027. Two related fights are moving in parallel: in December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's practice of deporting immigrants to third countries.rd countries that agree to adjudicate their asylum claims, and a third case could end the administration's attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings, NPR reports. For people with pending asylum claims, the practical position today is unchanged: their cases continue under the current rules while the court decides whether those rules were lawfully made.
